title: Korean prayer mountains
hook: Korean Christians rise before dawn for prayer meetings

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ethiopian, from a treasurer's chariot on a desert road to congregations across the continent. Your line was the center has moved. Whose voice from Africa did you listen to? Day nine hundred seventy-seven.

It's still dark outside, and the church lights are already on. In South Korea, some congregations meet for prayer before dawn on ordinary weekdays, before the subway fills and the offices open. People come in work clothes. Some kneel, some sit. Then the whole room starts praying out loud at once, each person in their own words, a sound like rain on a roof. Out of the cities, on the hillsides, there are places set apart only for prayer: prayer mountains, with small rooms and little caves where someone can go and pray through a night, or a week. Today, Korean prayer mountains, and the hour before the sun.

In Korean, the early meeting is called saebyeok gido, dawn prayer. There's a verse that fits the habit. Mark's Gospel describes one day in Jesus's life. The night before, the whole town had crowded his door. Then, in the King James Bible: "And in the morning, rising up a great while before day, he went out, and departed into a solitary place, and there prayed." Mark doesn't say what he prayed. Only when, and where: before day, and alone. A few lines later the disciples find him and say, "All men seek for thee." The prayer sits in the gap between the crowd last night and the crowd this morning. A psalm says the same thing from the other side: "My voice shalt thou hear in the morning, O LORD; in the morning will I direct my prayer unto thee, and will look up." Look up. Some readers hear a watchman on a wall, waiting for the light. Now put the two Korean habits beside Mark's verse. The prayer mountain takes his solitary place and gives it an address. People climb, sometimes fasting, pray in a small room cut into the hill, and come back down to their lives. The dawn meeting takes his early hour and gives it company. Two shapes of the same line: alone on a hill, and together in the dark. Not every Korean church keeps the dawn hour, and Christians pray at other hours too; nobody claims the morning is the only time for it. But the habit has a simple logic. Before the day has said a word to you, before the phone and the news and the list, the first words can go somewhere else.
screen: `IN THE MORNING, AND WILL LOOK UP.`
`ALONE ON A HILL, TOGETHER IN THE DARK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: borrow the dawn. If it's early where you are, good. If it isn't, this still works. Settle, and breathe. Go back in your mind to the first minute of today, before anything happened. What got there first? A worry, a screen, a list, someone else's voice? Don't scold yourself. Just notice. Now give the next two minutes the job the morning might have had. If you pray, you can borrow the psalm: in the morning will I direct my prayer unto thee. If you don't, sit facing a window if you can, look up, and wait, the way a watchman waits for light. The bell holds the time.
Saebyeok gido. Korean for dawn prayer, prayer that gets there before the day does, kept on hillsides and in city churches before sunrise.
Your line: dawn prayer. Tomorrow morning, before you check anything, give the first minute away: a prayer, a verse, or one long look at the sky. Day nine hundred seventy-seven.

howItsDone: In South Korea, some Protestant churches hold prayer meetings before dawn on weekdays, where the congregation may pray aloud together, and prayer retreats on hillsides let people go away to pray for a night or longer.

notes: Claims rule: no dates, counts or history of the Korean revivals given. The description of dawn prayer (saebyeok gido), praying aloud together (tongseong gido, not named) and prayer mountains (gidowon) with small rooms and caves is general; a Keeper familiar with Korean Protestant practice should confirm the picture, including 'sometimes fasting'.
Romanization 'saebyeok gido' (새벽기도) follows Revised Romanization; confirm.
'Ask the people who keep it why, and they will usually point you to a verse' is a generalization about practitioners; soften or cut if a Keeper prefers.
The 'watchman' image for 'look up' in Psalm 5:3 is an interpretive gloss (the Hebrew verb can mean to watch or keep watch); confirm it is fair.

Editor pass: review question now matches yesterday's carry (an African Christian voice) and drops the unsourced 'keeps shifting south'; cut the generalization that practitioners 'usually point you to a verse'; marked the watchman image as 'some readers'; replaced 'the morning is not the only time God listens' (narrator speaking for God) with a neutral line.
Original: πρωΐ in Mark 1:35 (πρωῒ ἔννυχα λίαν); confirm accent form and pronunciation.
Audit pass: 'Behind the habit sits a verse' asserted an unsourced origin for saebyeok gido; now 'There's a verse that fits the habit.' Quotations (Mark 1:35, 1:37; Psalm 5:3 KJV) checked exact.
